cases.text: How much juice is in a lime?
checks: Gives an approximate kitchen quantity with units; acknowledges size/juiciness variation
cases.raw_text:
A regular lime gives about 2 tablespoons of juice, or roughly 1 ounce. A small key lime gives only about 2 teaspoons.

===MORE===
Typical juice from one lime:
- Regular (Persian) lime, medium: about 2 tablespoons (1 oz or 30 ml). A small or dry one may give only 1 to 1½ tablespoons, and a large juicy one can give up to 3.
- Key lime: about 2 teaspoons (10 ml).

Rough conversions:
- 1/4 cup of juice takes about 2 regular limes.
- 1/2 cup takes about 4 regular limes.
- 1 cup takes about 8 regular limes, or about 20 to 25 key limes.
- 1 lime also gives about 2 teaspoons of grated zest.

To get more juice:
- Use room-temperature limes, or microwave one for 10 to 15 seconds.
- Roll it firmly on the counter before you cut it.
- Pick limes that feel heavy for their size and have smooth, thin skin that gives a little when pressed.
cases.spoken: A regular lime gives about 2 tablespoons of juice, or roughly 1 ounce. A small key lime gives only about 2 teaspoons.

cases.text: How should I serve an apple to a one-year-old, according to Solid Starts?
checks: Retrieves and attributes Solid Starts rather than inventing its recommendation
Age-appropriate preparation; does not recommend raw chunks or wedges for a one-year-old
Distinguishes the source's thin raw slices/grated options from soft cooked apple
cases.reference_notes: Checked 2026-09-12: source's 9+ month section permits cooked sections, grated raw apple, thin rounds or half-rounds, with or without skin. Whole apples discussed at 18+ months; wedges at 24+ months with readiness qualifications.
cases.raw_text:
Solid Starts treats apple as a choking risk at this age, so serve it soft or very thin. Use finely grated or paper-thin slices of raw apple, or apple cooked until soft and cut into small bite-size pieces, and save wedges for after age two.

===MORE===
Solid Starts' guidance on apple for babies around 12 months:

Ways to serve it:
- Grated raw apple: shred it finely and offer it on its own or mixed into foods like oatmeal or yogurt.
- Paper-thin raw slices: slice it so thin that it bends easily, not crunchy chunks.
- Cooked apple: steam, bake or sauté it until it's soft enough to squish between your fingers, then cut it into small bite-size pieces your toddler can pick up.
- Applesauce: spread it on toast or serve it with a spoon.

What to avoid:
- Raw apple wedges, quarters or chunks. Raw apple is hard and crisp, and Solid Starts lists it as a common choking hazard. Its apple page says most toddlers are ready for sections of raw apple sometime after their second birthday.
- Whole apples to bite from at this age.

Other notes:
- Solid Starts says small amounts of apple juice are fine as a drink after 12 months.
- Other feeding sites give similar advice for the 12-month age: Once Upon a Farm says paper-thin raw slices from 12 to 24 months, Michigan Apples suggests very thin matchstick strips about a quarter inch wide, and Yummy Toddler Food advises against thick raw slices until about age three.
- Always stay with your child while they eat.

The search couldn't load Solid Starts' full 12-month section, which is partly in their app. The serving styles listed here are based on their published apple page, but check the age-specific details in the app or at solidstarts.com/foods/apple.

Sources: solidstarts.com/foods/apple, Once Upon a Farm, Michigan Apples, Yummy Toddler Food.
cases.spoken: Solid Starts treats apple as a choking risk at this age, so serve it soft or very thin. Use finely grated or paper-thin slices of raw apple, or apple cooked until soft and cut into small bite-size pieces, and save wedges for after age two.

cases.text: What about with the skin on?
checks: Accurately represents the named source: skin is permitted for the thin raw slices in its 9+ month section
Does not turn skin permission into permission for thick raw pieces
cases.raw_text:
Yes, Solid Starts says the skin can stay on for a one-year-old as long as the slices are very thin or the apple is grated. If your toddler struggles with it, peel the apple or peel it in stripes.

===MORE===
What Solid Starts says about apple skin:
- From about 9 months, it suggests very thin slices of raw apple, either with the skin or without it.
- Leaving the skin on helps the slices hold together, so they're easier for little hands to grip.
- Chewing the skin, and spitting it out, helps your child build eating skills.
- If your toddler gags on the skin or can't manage it, peel the whole apple or peel off stripes to leave less skin.
- Always remove the core and seeds.

Why the advice is cautious:
- Raw apple is firm, hard to chew and can be slippery, so Solid Starts lists it as a choking risk.
- Some health agencies are stricter about the skin. The UK's NHS suggests removing fruit skin for very young children so it's easier to swallow. Ireland's HSE says to peel fruit and remove tough fibers and seeds.

What to do:
- Grated apple or paper-thin slices with the skin on are fine if your toddler is handling them well.
- Cooked apple that's soft enough to squish is easier to eat, with or without the skin.
- Don't serve thick wedges or chunks with the skin until after age two.
- Have your child sit upright while eating, and stay with them.

Sources: Solid Starts apple page (solidstarts.com/foods/apple), NHS "Preparing food safely," HSE "Food choking risks."
cases.spoken: Yes, Solid Starts says the skin can stay on for a one-year-old as long as the slices are very thin or the apple is grated. If your toddler struggles with it, peel the apple or peel it in stripes.

cases.text: Can I substitute baking soda for baking powder in pancakes?
checks: Explains not a direct one-for-one substitution
Baking soda needs acid; baking powder contains an acid component
Avoids prescribing an unconditional replacement ratio without recipe context
cases.raw_text:
Yes, but it needs an acid. Use about a quarter teaspoon of baking soda for every teaspoon of baking powder, and swap the milk for buttermilk or add a little lemon juice or vinegar.

===MORE===
Yes, you can, but baking soda works differently from baking powder.

Why it needs an acid
Baking powder is baking soda with an acid already mixed in. Baking soda alone only makes bubbles when it reacts with an acid. Without one, your pancakes will be flat and taste soapy or metallic.

How much to use
Baking soda is about 3 to 4 times stronger than baking powder.
- 1 tsp baking powder = 1/4 tsp baking soda plus an acid

Acid options (pick one)
- Use buttermilk instead of regular milk, one-for-one.
- Make quick "buttermilk" by adding 1 tbsp lemon juice or white vinegar to 1 cup of milk. Let it sit for 5 minutes.
- Use plain yogurt thinned with a little milk.
- Add 1/2 tsp cream of tartar plus 1/4 tsp baking soda for each 1 tsp of baking powder. Together they make a homemade baking powder, and you can keep using regular milk.

Tips
- Cook the batter soon after mixing. Baking soda reacts right away, so its bubbles fade if the batter sits.
- Don't add extra soda. Too much gives a bitter, soapy taste and can make the pancakes brown too fast.
cases.spoken: Yes, but it needs an acid. Use about a quarter teaspoon of baking soda for every teaspoon of baking powder, and swap the milk for buttermilk or add a little lemon juice or vinegar.

cases.text: When I mix blue and red light from an LED strip, I see purple. Are the waveforms collapsing to an average wavelength, the same as a single purple wavelength, or are my eyes seeing purple while red and blue are still emitted separately?
checks: Red and blue spectral components remain; ordinary LED mixing does not average them into a new wavelength
Explains additive color perception through cone responses and brain interpretation
Distinguishes nonspectral purple/magenta from spectral violet
Does not confuse superposition with nonlinear frequency conversion or quantum collapse
cases.raw_text:
Your eyes are making the purple. The red and blue light stay as two separate wavelengths, and there's no single "purple wavelength" that matches what you're seeing.

===MORE===
The light itself:
- Light waves don't merge or average out. Red light (about 620–630 nm) and blue light (about 450–470 nm) pass through the same space without changing each other.
- A spectrometer pointed at your LED strip would show two separate peaks, one red and one blue, with nothing in between.
- If the wavelengths did average, you'd get about 540–550 nm, which is green. That's clearly not what you see.

What your eyes and brain do:
- Your retina has three types of color-sensing cones: short (blue), medium (green) and long (red).
- Red plus blue light strongly triggers the short and long cones while leaving the medium cones mostly unstimulated.
- Your brain reads that pattern as purple or magenta.

Why no single wavelength matches:
- Single wavelengths run in a line from violet through blue, green, yellow and orange to red. Each one stimulates cones that sit next to each other on that line.
- No single wavelength can strongly stimulate both the short and long cones while skipping the medium ones in between. That's why magenta and red-purple aren't in the rainbow. Color scientists call them "non-spectral" colors.
- Violet (about 400 nm) is a real single wavelength and can look a bit like purple, but it's a different color. The purple from your LED strip is mostly made by your brain.

This also explains why RGB LED strips work at all. They don't produce every wavelength. They mix three colors to trigger your three cone types in different amounts, and your brain fills in the rest. Yellow from an RGB strip works the same way: it's red and green light together, with no yellow wavelength in it.
cases.spoken: Your eyes are making the purple. The red and blue light stay as two separate wavelengths, and there's no single "purple wavelength" that matches what you're seeing.
